surveyDefinition.title: Smartwatches — consumer survey (Canada)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on smartwatch ownership, usage intensity, purchase drivers, and unmet needs.

segments.name: Health-Monitoring Owners
segments.description: Own a smartwatch primarily to track continuous health metrics — heart rate, sleep stages, SpO2 — and wear it day and night. They are frustrated by battery life that fails to last through the night and by questionable accuracy of health data.

segments.name: Fitness-Performance Users
segments.description: Use the smartwatch mainly for structured workouts and training — they need reliable heart rate during HIIT, GPS, and a screen that is easy to interact with mid-exercise. They are less concerned with style and more with ruggedness and real-time data.

segments.name: Ecosystem-Committed Users
segments.description: Bought the smartwatch to stay connected to their phone's ecosystem — notifications, calls, and seamless integration with their existing devices. They are brand-loyal and less price-sensitive, but resent subscription fees for features they feel should be included.

segments.name: Occasional Notification Users
segments.description: Wear the smartwatch mainly for notifications and basic step counting, not for deep health or fitness tracking. They are the least engaged, may not wear it daily, and are price-sensitive — they see the watch as a convenience rather than a necessity.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Smartwatches buyers in Canada. It asks how people use Smartwatches, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in Canada who buy or use Smartwatches for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who currently own or have purchased a smartwatch in the past 12 months; Individuals who are actively considering purchasing a smartwatch within the next 6 months; Adults aged 18+ who make their own purchase decisions. Excluded: Businesses or institutions purchasing smartwatches in bulk for employees; Children under 18 (unless the study specifically targets kids' smartwatches, which is not the primary market); Individuals who only use basic fitness bands without smart features.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Consumers buy smartwatches for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide on the model and brand themselves. While some businesses may purchase smartwatches for employees, the dominant and defining purchase is by individual consumers, making this a pure B2C market.
respondentBehaviours: Health and fitness tracking (steps, heart rate, sleep)
Smartphone integration for notifications and calls
Brand loyalty to smartphone ecosystems (Apple, Samsung, etc.)
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are modelled estimates built from published market evidence — they are not measurements from fielded interviews, and should be read as an expected shape of response rather than a result. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing who owns a smartwatch and how they use it day-to-day — frequency, overnight wear, and the mix of health, fitness, and notification use. It then moves into the purchase journey: what triggered the buy, where they researched and bought, what they paid, and what decided the choice. Next it probes their expectations and preferences — must-have features, battery and charging, app experience, trade-offs, and value tolerance. It closes with satisfaction, pain points, switching triggers, and future upgrade intent. This arc separates the four segments by their primary…

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Smartwatches in Canada — who Individuals who currently own or have purchased a smartwatch in the past 12 months; Individuals who are actively considering purchasing a smartwatch within the next 6 months; Adults aged 18+ who make their own purchase decisions. The audience is defined as individual consumers who buy smartwatches for personal use, as they are the primary purchasers and decision-makers. The demographic and behavioral criteria capture both current owners and potential buyers to support a broad consumer survey.

metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on smartwatch ownership, usage intensity, purchase drivers, and unmet needs.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Jobs-to-be-done combined with usage intensity: the primary axis is what the smartwatch is hired to do (health monitoring, fitness, connectivity, style) because the same device serves fundamentally different needs, and usage intensity separates heavy daily users from occasional ones. This fits better

segments.name: Health-Monitoring Owners
segments.description: Own a smartwatch primarily to track continuous health metrics — heart rate, sleep stages, SpO2 — and wear it day and night. They are frustrated by battery life that fails to last through the night and by questionable accuracy of health data.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report high daily wear time, prioritise battery life and sensor accuracy above all else, and be willing to pay more for advanced health features.

segments.name: Fitness-Performance Users
segments.description: Use the smartwatch mainly for structured workouts and training — they need reliable heart rate during HIIT, GPS, and a screen that is easy to interact with mid-exercise. They are less concerned with style and more with ruggedness and real-time data.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report frequent workout-specific usage, cite accuracy during exercise as a top pain point, and be open to switching for better fitness features.

segments.name: Ecosystem-Committed Users
segments.description: Bought the smartwatch to stay connected to their phone's ecosystem — notifications, calls, and seamless integration with their existing devices. They are brand-loyal and less price-sensitive, but resent subscription fees for features they feel should be included.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report high satisfaction with brand integration, low likelihood of switching to a different ecosystem, and high irritation with subscription paywalls.

segments.name: Occasional Notification Users
segments.description: Wear the smartwatch mainly for notifications and basic step counting, not for deep health or fitness tracking. They are the least engaged, may not wear it daily, and are price-sensitive — they see the watch as a convenience rather than a necessity.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report lower usage frequency, fewer health features used, and higher price sensitivity, and they will be the most likely to lapse or not repurchase.

segmentModel.tie_break: The question 'Which of these problems bothers you most with your current smartwatch?' (sf3) is the most direct behavioural self-report because it asks respondents to pick their single biggest pain point, which cleanly separates health-monitoring owners (battery/accuracy), fitness users (screen during workouts), and ecosystem users (subscription fees).
notes: Occasional notification users are identified by low engagement (cp2, cp3, cp5) and notification-focused purchase reasons (bb1, bb2) plus price sensitivity (bb7).
Health-monitoring owners are strongly identified by overnight wear (cp3, cp5) and sleep/health pain points (sf3, sf5).
Fitness-performance users are identified by workout usage (cp6) and workout-specific pain points (sf3, sf5).
Ecosystem-committed users are identified by brand integration priorities (bb8, pe1) and subscription fee resentment (pe8, sf3, sf5).
13 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are modelled from published market evidence, not measured from fielded interviews. Replace them with primary data once the study is run.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing who owns a smartwatch and how they use it day-to-day — frequency, overnight wear, and the mix of health, fitness, and notification use. It then moves into the purchase journey: what triggered the buy, where they researched and bought, what they paid, and what decided the choice. Next it probes their expectations and preferences — must-have features, battery and charging, app experience, trade-offs, and value tolerance. It closes with satisfaction, pain points, switching triggers, and future upgrade intent. This arc separates the four segments by their primary…
storyline_notes: Replaced the generic 'category relationship' opening with a smartwatch-specific ownership and brand ecosystem question, since the category is defined by which phone ecosystem the watch belongs to.
Added a dedicated 'battery and charging' beat in preferences because battery life is the top pain point in the market and is central to segment separation (health monitors need overnight wear).
Added a 'value expectation' beat that explicitly covers subscription fees, a major source of frustration and a differentiator between price-sensitive and committed users.

In the buying section, kept 'price paid' separate from 'decision drivers' because price sensitivity is a key segment axis, and the region's medium price sensitivity means it must be measured directly.
In satisfaction, combined 'switching triggers' and 'future intent' to capture both the pull factors (features) and the push factors (pain points) that drive upgrade or brand change.

The beats are designed so that segment assignment can be derived from: primary use case (health vs fitness vs notifications), wear frequency (daily/nightly vs occasional), and responses to battery/subscription trade-offs.
metadata.classification_reason: Consumers buy smartwatches for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide on the model and brand themselves. While some businesses may purchase smartwatches for employees, the dominant and defining purchase is by individual consumers, making this a pure B2C market.
